8/20/2026
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
V. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC.;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

PLAINTIFF’S PROTECTIVE OPPOSITION TO THE MOTION TO DISMISS
OF DEFENDANT NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING &
EXPLOITED CHILDREN

Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine files this opposition protectively: it demonstrates that the
First Amended Complaint (“FAC”) states its claims on the facts already pleaded, without awaiting,
and without prejudice to, Plaintiff’s forthcoming motion for leave to file a supplemental pleading
under Rule 15(d). Citations to “Mem.” refer to NCMEC’s August 12, 2026 Memorandum in
Support.

I. INTRODUCTION

“You got exactly what you asked for.”

Counsel for the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children wrote those words to

Plaintiff on August 13, 2026. That same day, Plaintiff had asked three closed questions: whether

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 2 of 14 PagelD# 262

the two CyberTipline reports NCMEC invoked identified him by his legal name, by the name he
uses, or by an email identifier. Counsel answered none of them. What counsel wrote instead went
to a Plaintiff whose pleaded injuries NCMEC had recited in its own memorandum one day earlier.

The refusal matters because it is the motion. NCMEC’s April 22 letters stated that two

3 66

CyberTipline reports concerned “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” “Jay Ballentine,” “and/or” an email
identifier. NCMEC’s motion says less. It tells the Court the reports may be linked to Plaintiff, “a
person with the same name,” or an email address—while emphasizing that Plaintiff “does not have
access to those reports.” NCMEC holds the records that resolve that ambiguity. NCMEC declines
to resolve it. NCMEC now asks the Court to convert Plaintiff’s lack of access to NCMEC’s own
records into dismissal with prejudice.

The same posture appears on the other coast. In Plaintiff’s California action, Meta
Platforms, Inc. filed a motion the same day invoking its child-safety enforcement policy while
omitting that Meta is a named and served defendant here under the first clause of 42 U.S.C. §
1985(2). Meta cites this case but omits its role in it. NCMEC invokes the reports but will not say
whom they concern. Each defendant claims the protection of the same child-safety apparatus.
Neither will answer the identity question their own positions have made dispositive.

The answer NCMEC will not give is the answer its truth argument requires. Without it, the
motion reduces to one question: whether the First Amended Complaint states claims on the facts
actually pleaded. It does. The motion should be denied.

II. ISSUES TO BE DECIDED

1. NCMEC asks the Court to dismiss this case on litigation privilege and statutory

immunity. Those defenses depend on facts. May NCMEC obtain dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6)

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 3 of 14 PagelD# 263

when the First Amended Complaint does not establish the predicates those defenses require — and
pleads facts bringing the April 22, 2026 letters within the statutory exceptions?

2. NCMEC says its letters were true. May NCMEC establish truth at the pleading
stage with the letters alone, when the Complaint pleads that their imputation is false and the letters
never identify which person or identifier either report concerns?

3. Do the pleaded facts — what the letters said, the CyberTipline context in which they
said it, when they issued, to whom they went, and what came before them — plausibly state
Plaintiff’s claims for defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and conspiracy?

Il. LEGAL STANDARD

A motion under Rule 12(b)(6) tests the legal sufficiency of the complaint. The Court
accepts well-pleaded factual allegations as true, draws all reasonable inferences in Plaintiff’s favor,
and does not resolve disputed facts. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co. v. Kolon Indus., Inc., 637 F.3d
435, 440 (4th Cir. 2011).

An affirmative defense ordinarily cannot be resolved on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion. The
exception is rare, and it exists only when all facts necessary to establish the defense clearly appear
on the face of the complaint. Goodman v. Praxair, Inc., 494 F.3d 458, 464 (4th Cir. 2007) (en
banc). This Court applied that rule in SkyBell Technologies, Inc. v. Alarm.com, Inc., No. 1:25-cv-
01105-RDA-WBP (E.D. Va. Mar. 4, 2026), ECF No. 32, declining to resolve a defense that turned
on facts the pleadings did not settle.

IV. ARGUMENT

A. NCMEC Cannot Establish Privilege, Statutory Immunity, or Truth on This

Pleading.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 4 of 14 PagelD# 264

NCMEC’s first three arguments share one structure: each asks the Court to adopt a
predicate that the Rule 12 record does not establish. The subsections below identify each predicate
in turn.

1. Litigation Privilege

Virginia’s absolute judicial privilege reaches some communications made outside the
courtroom and can reach qualifying communications preliminary to contemplated litigation.
Mansfield v. Bernabei, 284 Va. 116, 727 S.E.2d 69 (2012). A court in this district has resolved the
privilege at the pleading stage. Daniczek v. Spencer, 156 F. Supp. 3d 739 (E.D. Va. 2016). The
question is whether, accepting the FAC’s facts as true, Virginia law establishes that these particular
communications fall within the absolute privilege. It does not.

NCMEC acknowledges that its counsel has identified no clear holding of the Fourth Circuit
or its member districts extending absolute privilege to subpoena responses. Mem. at 5. And on the
pleaded facts, the letters were not part of compelled judicial process: no subpoena had been served,
no court order required a response, Plaintiff had not waived service or requested an early answer,
and the announced notice period had not run. FAC {J 71, 73. The letters were voluntary
correspondence sent to Plaintiff alone, filed with no tribunal, and copied to no counsel of record,
FAC 4 78; each opened by invoking compulsory force that did not then exist, FAC 70; and each
issued while motions directed at the same discovery remained pending, FAC ¢ 72. The FAC
predicates no liability on any court filing. FAC 4 25. The absence of service matters not because
service is an element of the privilege, but because it separates these letters from compelled judicial
process — and from the subpoena-response authorities NCMEC assembles from other

jurisdictions.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 5 of 14 PagelD# 265

NCMEC answers with waiver: recipients may respond to a subpoena without formal
service, and a failure to serve “is not a prohibition against response.” Mem. at 6. That answers a
different question. Permission to respond is not the question. Absolute immunity from tort liability
is. The proposition that NCMEC was free to volunteer information does not establish the separate
proposition that Virginia law makes the resulting communication absolutely privileged. On the
pleaded facts, and on the authority NCMEC itself describes, the privilege is not established.

2. Statutory Immunity

Immunity under 18 U.S.C. § 2258D is qualified, as NCMEC’s own Memorandum
recognizes. Mem. at 7. It reaches claims arising from the performance of CyberTipline
responsibilities or functions, and it yields to exceptions for intentional misconduct; for actual
malice or reckless disregard of a substantial risk of causing injury without legal justification; for
action taken for a purpose unrelated to the specified statutory functions; and for ordinary business
activity. 18 U.S.C. § 2258D(a)-(c).

The FAC does not concede the predicate. It pleads that neither letter was a CyberTipline
report, a referral or disclosure to law enforcement, or any reporting, preservation, or disclosure
function described in 18 U.S.C. §§ 2258A—2258C — that the challenged act was voluntary legal
correspondence issued without any served subpoena or court order. FAC 4 79. It pleads, in the
alternative, facts within the statutory exceptions: a knowingly false invocation of compulsory
process, issuance without obligation of any kind, wording Hall selected and controlled, and timing
keyed to pending motions and imminent depositions. FAC {J 70—74, 79, 85-86.

The sequence matters. NCMEC must show that the challenged conduct falls within the
protected statutory function. The FAC pleads facts distinguishing that function from the

correspondence at issue and pleads exception facts in the alternative. NCMEC’s contrary

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 6 of 14 PagelD# 266

characterization requires the Court to choose NCMEC’s version of the letters over the version
pleaded. Goodman forecloses that choice. The Court need not classify the conduct now. It need
only decline to accept NCMEC’s classification as fact.

Immunity under 34 U.S.C. § 20505 is worded differently and must be answered on its own
terms. It bars specified reputational claims arising from actions or communications “in connection
with” a clearinghouse, hotline, or complaint intake or forwarding program, unless the plaintiff
shows actual malice or that the information or action was provided or taken for a purpose unrelated
to an activity mandated by federal law. 34 U.S.C. § 20505. It contains no ordinary-business
exception and no separately stated reckless-disregard exception. The FAC pleads facts within both
of the exceptions it does contain. It alleges actual malice: Hall invoked a subpoena that had not
been served and that compelled nothing, and she selected wording associating Plaintiff personally
with the reports although the identifiers were supplied by Plaintiff, linked disjunctively, and
accompanied by no report-specific match or disambiguation. FAC {f 85, 191-192. And it alleges a
purpose unrelated to any activity mandated by federal law: the letters implemented no reporting,
referral, preservation, or disclosure function, and their alleged purpose was to deter Plaintiff from
attending and testifying in the two federal actions. FAC {§ 79, 156, 162. On those allegations, §
20505, like § 2258D, is not established on the face of the pleading.

3. Truth

NCMEC reframes the falsity alleged. The FAC does not depend on proving that NCMEC
possessed no records responsive to any one of three search terms. It alleges that NCMEC falsely
published a person-level association between Plaintiff and child-exploitation reports. FAC J{ 99-—

101, 189, 210.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 7 of 14 PagelD# 267

The letters stated that NCMEC had received two CyberTipline reports “concerning”
Plaintiff’s legal name, the name he uses, “and/or” an email identifier. They did not identify which
listed identifier corresponded to either report. FAC § 92. They did not state whether any identifier
appeared in a provider-submitted report or was instead drawn from Plaintiff’s own April 9
materials. FAC { 77, 95. They did not state that the three identifiers describe one person, and “Jay
Ballentine” is not alleged to be unique. FAC 94, 96. The FAC pleads that the personal
imputation each letter conveyed is false. FAC 4 101.

At this stage, the Court credits a pleaded allegation of falsity unless it is conclusory or
contradicted by a document properly before the Court. See Dangerfield v. WAVY Broadcasting,
LLC, 228 F. Supp. 3d 696, 701-02 (E.D. Va. 2017). No underlying CyberTipline report is before
the Court. The April 9 materials NCMEC attaches establish what Plaintiff asked; the April 22
letters establish what NCMEC published; neither establishes which person or identifier actually
appears in either source report. And Goines forecloses the use NCMEC makes of the letters.
Consideration of a document at Rule 12 does not mean the plaintiff adopts the truth of its contents
— arule that exists precisely because treating every attached writing as true would let the allegedly
libelous publication plead the plaintiff out of court. Goines v. Valley Cmty. Servs. Bd., 822 F.3d
159, 167-69 (4th Cir. 2016). The letters establish what NCMEC published. They do not establish
that what NCMEC published was true. NCMEC’s own Memorandum states that Plaintiff “does not
have access to those reports” while describing the possible referent as Plaintiff, “a person with the
same name,” or an email address. Mem. at 9. The truth theory presents a disputed factual predicate,
not a basis for Rule 12 dismissal.

B. The Pleaded Words and Context State Defamation and Insulting-Words

Claims.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 8 of 14 PagelD# 268

The letters state:

“NCMEC has received two (2) CyberTipline reports concerning (1) Marvelle J.

Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level identifier

jaychizza@icloud.com between July 1, 2022 and the present.”

The question is whether those words, read in the pleaded context, are reasonably capable of
the meaning the FAC alleges. The FAC supplies that context. Reports to the CyberTipline concern
apparent violations of enumerated federal child-exploitation statutes. FAC { 97-98. The
statement says the reports are “concerning” the listed names and identifier; it does not say that a
search of records produced results. Plaintiff’s full legal name appears first on the list. The
disjunctive “and/or” never identifies the actual match, and nothing in either letter separates
Plaintiff from the reports or attributes them to a different person. FAC {{ 92, 95-96. The FAC
pleads the resulting imputation and its falsity. FAC 4 99-101.

Dangerfield does not carry the weight NCMEC assigns it. There, the court could determine
what the words “accused of rape” communicated, and the incorporated warrant materials showed
that the accusation had in fact been made. 228 F. Supp. 3d at 701-02. Here, NCMEC’s own
Memorandum preserves the ambiguity the letters created, describing the referent as Plaintiff, a
person with the same name, or an email address. Mem. at 9. That ambiguity does not itself establish
liability. It defeats NCMEC’s contention that the publication is incapable, as a matter of law, of the
pleaded implication. As to authorial intent, the FAC alleges that Hall selected the wording; that she
invoked a subpoena as the basis for the response when that subpoena had not been served and
compliance had not been compelled; and that the identifiers were supplied by Plaintiff, linked
disjunctively, and accompanied by no report-specific match or disambiguation — circumstances

from which intent to convey the implication is inferred. FAC {J 85, 191-192, 212-213.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 9 of 14 PagelD# 269

Count VI requires little more. NCMEC argues that the insulting-words claim rises or falls
with the defamation theory. Mem. at 11. Accepting that premise for purposes of this Motion, the
conclusion follows: because NCMEC has not established that the defamation theory fails, its
derivative argument against Count VI fails with it.

C. Count III Plausibly Alleges Intentional Infliction of Emotional Distress.

NCMEC reduces Count III to the act of “responding to the subpoenas.” Mem. at 12. Rule
12 requires the Court to evaluate the conduct actually pleaded, and the FAC pleads a combination
of circumstances, not a subpoena response.

Hall was NCMEC’s Corporate Counsel. FAC { 80. The FAC alleges that she understood
the criminal and law-enforcement significance of associating a named individual with
CyberTipline reports, FAC {§ 61, 224; that before the letters issued she had reviewed, or received
from participants in the two actions, materials disclosing that Plaintiff is a survivor of childhood
sexual abuse who had already been injured by association with the language of child exploitation,
FAC 4 39-45, 60, 225; and that she possessed the case-specific materials identifying the two
actions, the identifiers, and the discovery at issue, FAC §§ 59, 87. On that footing, the FAC alleges,
Hall issued two case-keyed letters with no subpoena served, no waiver, no court order, and no
request for an early answer — one day after motions directed at the same discovery and before any
ruling on them — transmitted to Plaintiff alone, opening with a false invocation of compulsory
process, and substituting an unsworn, source-free assertion for the sworn examination then days
away. FAC ff 68, 70—73, 76, 78, 226.

The distress pleaded is concrete. Upon reading the letters, Plaintiff vomited, experienced
recurrent involuntary recollections of his own childhood sexual abuse, lived in acute fear of

imminent arrest and prosecution, distanced himself from his own children because he expected to

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 _ Filed 08/20/26 Page 10 of 14 PagelD#
270

be taken into custody by law enforcement, could not maintain ordinary sleep or eating, could not
sustain attention on litigation materials, and refrained from dismissing his two federal actions only
by deliberate effort. FAC §§ 171-173, 229, 231. That exceeds a bare assertion of severe distress.

Virginia confines this tort to conduct that is outrageous and intolerable, and the standard is
not satisfied lightly. SuperValu, Inc. v. Johnson, 276 Va. 356, 370 (2008). But whether the pleaded
combination — directing at a disclosed survivor of childhood sexual abuse a false, source-
unidentified assertion tying his name to child-exploitation reporting, under color of compulsory
force that did not then exist, timed to the same discovery then pending — crosses that threshold is
answered on the allegations as pleaded, taken together, not on NCMEC’s shortened description of
them. FAC 9 226-227. Count III states a claim.

D. The Conspiracy Counts Plead Agreement Through Particular Facts, Not

Labels.

The rule NCMEC cites is not in dispute: parallel conduct plus a bare assertion of agreement
does not state a conspiracy claim. A Soc’y Without a Name v. Virginia, 655 F.3d 342, 346 (4th Cir.
2011). That rule does not describe this pleading.

The FAC alleges particulars. As of April 9, 2026, NCMEC and counsel for Meta and
Accenture had received identical case-specific materials identifying the same two federal actions,
the same three identifiers, and the same discovery objective. FAC 4 57-58, 124. On April 21, the
defendants in those actions moved to stop the identified discovery. FAC { 63-67, 125.
Depositions covering the report-existence question were noticed for April 28 through April 30.
FAC 4 50-52, 126. On April 22 — under no compulsion of any kind — Hall issued two separate
letters, each keyed by caption and case number to one of the two actions, before service, before the

requested ruling dates, and before the depositions. FAC {ff 68, 127-129. The letters supplied,

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 11 of 14 PagelD#
271

outside the discovery process, an unswom and source-free assertion on the exact question
scheduled for sworn examination. FAC ff 131, 133. And the identities and communications that
would establish the details of the agreement rest in Defendants’ records, not Plaintiff’s. FAC 4 134.

These allegations do not prove agreement, and at this stage they need not. They are concrete
circumstances from which agreement may plausibly be inferred. NCMEC’s argument asks the
Court to select NCMEC’s innocent explanation over the inference Rule 12 requires the Court to
draw in Plaintiff’s favor.

The FAC also pleads the statutory object of Count IV. It alleges that the purpose of the
agreement was to deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from continuing to attend the two federal actions
as a party and from testifying freely, fully, and truthfully as a prospective witness in them, with the
April 22, 2026 letters as the means. FAC §§ 156-157, 162, 235.

The common-law count follows. The FAC pleads combination, underlying tortious
conduct, overt acts, time and sequence, purpose, and resulting injury. FAC {{ 156, 163-166, 243—
248. Because the underlying defamation claims survive this Motion, NCMEC cannot obtain
dismissal of Count V by declaring the alleged agreement implausible. See Almy v. Grisham, 273
Va. 68, 80 (2007).

E. Dismissal With Prejudice Would Be Unwarranted.

NCMEC requests dismissal with prejudice, citing the prior action and the single
amendment here. Mem. at 17. The prior action ended in a voluntary dismissal without any merits
adjudication. The present FAC reflects one amendment, not repeated failures to cure deficiencies
identified by any court. NCMEC’s claim that amendment would be futile depends on the same
Rule 12 arguments addressed above. If the Court were to identify a curable deficiency, dismissal

with prejudice would require a recognized basis under Rule 15 — such as repeated failure to cure

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document 20 Filed 08/20/26 Page 12 of 14 PagelD#
272

by amendments previously allowed — that this record does not present. Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S.
178, 182 (1962).

V. CONCLUSION

The Motion should be denied. In the alternative, any dismissal should be without prejudice

and with leave to amend.
